   Take Thursday . He held a press conference and was asked about his friendship with Tucker Carlson. Carlson, once a huge Trump supporter, has had a massive fallout with Trump, in part because of the Iran War. Vance stood by his friendship with Carlson (which has unnerved a lot of Jewish Republicans ) while also saying he disagrees with Carlson on many things (though he didn’t specify what).

   Take Monday . Trump said people who oppose data centers are “backwards and poor.” Asked about this, Vance didn’t call anyone names. Instead, he said the issue is concerns about rising utility bills.

   Also Monday, Vance got into a verbal UFC fight with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

   Allllllso Monday, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who is very close with Vance, resigned after repeatedly clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Asked Thursday if the Iran War would be over by the midterms, Vance replied, “I don’t know.”

   Vance has won some plaudits for the way he’s navigating it all. 

   “JD Vance is showing he can lead our entire movement in 2028,” Matt Gaetz wrote on social media .

   Presidential races start when they start. Not when you are ready for them to start.

   Importantly, Vance said nice things Thursday about Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Sen. Ted Cruz (R., Texas), whose names have recently been tossed around as part of the 2028 presidential sweepstakes.

   Running for president as vice president is both a blessing and a curse. Just ask Al Gore and Kamala Harris. Joe Biden was able to win after a four-year hiatus, but Mike Pence had no success. 

   Vance is going to have to build a coalition that is different from Trump’s while still staying in the president’s good graces. And he’ll have to do it while a number of other Republicans, like Cruz, are openly auditioning for the job and for Trump’s blessing.

   Still, Vance has a built-in advantage. He will have a prime opportunity next week to electrify GOP voters at the midterm convention in Dallas. The big question is, which speaking slot will he have at the 2028 GOP convention across the state in Houston?

Vance’s 2028 Audition With Voters Has Begun
 
Plus, Sen. Fetterman is showing little interest in his job, and some Republicans worry about having Trump at the center of their midterms campaign
 
 
ANNABELLE GORDON/UPI/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Good morning. The past couple of weeks have shown the gauntlet Vice President JD Vance will have to navigate if he seeks to sew up the GOP nomination for president in 2028.

 

He will need to stay close to President Trump while also owning the fact that he is not President Trump.

 

Take Thursday. He held a press conference and was asked about his friendship with Tucker Carlson. Carlson, once a huge Trump supporter, has had a massive fallout with Trump, in part because of the Iran War. Vance stood by his friendship with Carlson (which has unnerved a lot of Jewish Republicans) while also saying he disagrees with Carlson on many things (though he didn’t specify what).

 

Take Monday. Trump said people who oppose data centers are “backwards and poor.” Asked about this, Vance didn’t call anyone names. Instead, he said the issue is concerns about rising utility bills.

 

Also Monday, Vance got into a verbal UFC fight with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

 

Allllllso Monday, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who is very close with Vance, resigned after repeatedly clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Asked Thursday if the Iran War would be over by the midterms, Vance replied, “I don’t know.”

 

Vance has won some plaudits for the way he’s navigating it all. 

 

“JD Vance is showing he can lead our entire movement in 2028,” Matt Gaetz wrote on social media.

 

Presidential races start when they start. Not when you are ready for them to start.

 

Importantly, Vance said nice things Thursday about Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Sen. Ted Cruz (R., Texas), whose names have recently been tossed around as part of the 2028 presidential sweepstakes.

 

Running for president as vice president is both a blessing and a curse. Just ask Al Gore and Kamala Harris. Joe Biden was able to win after a four-year hiatus, but Mike Pence had no success. 

 

Vance is going to have to build a coalition that is different from Trump’s while still staying in the president’s good graces. And he’ll have to do it while a number of other Republicans, like Cruz, are openly auditioning for the job and for Trump’s blessing.

 

Still, Vance has a built-in advantage. He will have a prime opportunity next week to electrify GOP voters at the midterm convention in Dallas. The big question is, which speaking slot will he have at the 2028 GOP convention across the state in Houston?

 

There will be no Politics Newsletter on Monday in observance of Labor Day.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Randy Mastro: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s chief antagonist is a litigator who stared down the mob.

 

Jobs: August’s jobs data will be released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics at 8:30 a.m. ET.

 

Diesel prices: U.S. diesel prices jumped to a record high Friday as global supplies continue to tighten.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president heads to his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., this morning. In the afternoon he will have a policy meeting and sign executive orders.

What I’m Following

 
 
EVELYN HOCKSTEIN/REUTERS
 

John Fetterman is showing little interest in being a senator. The Pennsylvanian whose blue-collar wardrobe and plain-spoken progressivism made him a star is showing increasingly little interest in doing the work of his job, according to interviews with people close to him and a review of text messages and other internal records.

 

Some Republicans are growing wary of Trump being at the center of their midterms campaign. Congressional Republican leaders are putting Trump front and center in their campaign to keep control of the House and Senate. But some in the party say that strategy could set them up for a drubbing in the midterms.

 

Lawyers trying to sue the administration are coming up against the same problem. The Supreme Court’s decision this week to allow construction to continue on Trump’s ballroom highlights a recurring problem for lawyers seeking to sue his administration. When it comes to some of his most legally audacious actions, the biggest question for potential challengers isn’t whether they can win in court; it’s whether they meet the criteria to even sue.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The shock defection of two Democrats on a Republican procedural vote has sparked soul-searching in the party.

 

• The Trump administration has gone to the Supreme Court to try to lift the latest halt on new rules for mail ballots.

 

• An internal investigation concluded that former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer oversaw a ‘toxic, intimidating’ workplace and that she had an inappropriate relationship with a security staffer.

 

• The Netherlands has moved gold from New York to London, citing geopolitical unrest.

 

• The IRS is seeking to remove schools’ tax-exempt status if they consider race in any way, marking the latest in Trump’s push to reshape higher education.
